name: Witch hazel
habitat: Understorey shrub of eastern North American deciduous woodland, often on stream banks and slopes.
identify: Large shrub or small tree with wavy-toothed, asymmetric oval leaves — the leaf base is noticeably lopsided.
THE MARK: spidery yellow flowers with four narrow crinkled straps, opening in LATE AUTUMN or winter, often on bare branches. Almost nothing else flowers then.
Woody seed capsules that split and fling their seeds several metres.

lookalikes.name: Hazel
lookalikes.danger: Low; a harmless and unrelated shrub.
lookalikes.tell: Hazel has rounded, doubly-toothed, symmetric leaves, spring catkins and edible nuts. The late-autumn strap-petalled flower is unique to witch hazel.

lookalikes.name: Alder
lookalikes.tell: Alder carries small woody cone-like fruits and grows in wetter ground; the leaf base is symmetric.

preparations.method: Simmer chopped bark and twigs 20 minutes, strain, and cool.
preparations.for_use: An astringent wash for grazes, bruising, haemorrhoids and insect bites — it tightens tissue and slows capillary ooze.

preparations.method: Soak cloth in the cooled decoction.

cautions: Topical use is the well-attested one. Internal use of strong tannin preparations irritates the gut and, sustained, the kidneys.
The commercial distillate contains almost no tannin — it is not the same preparation as a bark decoction, whatever the label suggests.
It is a capillary astringent, not a treatment for a wound that is bleeding freely.
evidence: A long-standing official topical astringent, with pharmacopoeia monographs and reasonable evidence for skin inflammation. The distillate/decoction distinction is real and often ignored.
